subject: forensic-medicine
title: Thanatology: Postmortem Lividity, Rigor Mortis and Cadaveric Spasm

steps.title: Mechanism and development of postmortem lividity
steps.tx: Following cessation of circulation, gravity produces **postmortem lividity gravitational settling** (livor mortis or hypostasis) as red blood cells settle into dependent, uncompressed capillaries and venules. Lividity begins as mottled violaceous patches within one to two hours, coalesces into extensive confluent sheets by three to four hours, and becomes fully established and fixed between six and eight hours after death.
steps.say: Postmortem lividity is the purple staining of low skin areas caused by gravity pulling blood into capillaries, becoming fixed by eight hours.

nodes.label: Arrest of cardiac pump allows blood to settle under gravity
Mottled purplish patches appear in dependent areas (1 to 2 hours)
Patches coalesce into confluent purple sheets (3 to 4 hours)
Hemolysis causes tissue fixation of pigment (6 to 8 hours)

steps.title: Contact pallor and shifting of lividity
steps.tx: Areas where body weight compresses superficial dermal vessels exhibit **contact pallor pressure blanching**. When a body lies supine, the shoulder blades, buttocks, posterior thighs, and calves remain pale, outlined by surrounding purple lividity. Before fixation at six hours, turning the body causes blood to drain into newly dependent parts; after fixation, lividity remains permanently fixed in its initial position.
steps.say: Contact areas like shoulder blades and buttocks stay pale from pressure. Before six hours, moving the body shifts the color; after six hours, it is permanently fixed.

left.title: Before fixation (< 6 hours)
points: Blood remains within vessel lumens
Digital pressure blanches purple color completely
Flipping body causes lividity to drain to new side
Dual lividity absent

right.title: After fixation (> 6-8 hours)
points: Hemoglobin diffuses into extravascular dermis
Digital thumb pressure produces no blanching
Flipping body leaves original lividity unchanged
Can reveal that body was moved post-mortem

steps.title: Diagnostic color variations in toxic deaths
steps.tx: While normal postmortem hypostasis appears dark reddish-purple, **toxicological lividity color variations** provide pathognomonic diagnostic clues regarding fatal chemical poisoning. Carbon monoxide poisoning produces characteristic cherry-red lividity due to carboxyhemoglobin. Cyanide poisoning produces bright pink or brick-red lividity. Ingestion of potassium chlorate, nitrites, or aniline produces chocolate-brown lividity from methemoglobin, while phosphorus poisoning produces dark brown discoloration.
steps.say: Poisoning alters lividity color: carbon monoxide causes cherry-red staining, cyanide produces bright pink, and chlorates cause chocolate-brown color.

rows: High venous oxyhaemoglobin from cytochrome inhibition
Impaired oxygen dissociation in cold tissues

steps.title: Differentiating contusion from postmortem lividity
steps.tx: A vital postmortem dilemma involves the **contusion versus postmortem lividity** distinction. A contusion (bruise) represents antemortem trauma with ruptured blood vessels and extravasated blood clotted in subcutaneous tissues. To distinguish them, the pathologist makes a surgical incision: in lividity, intravascular blood washes away easily with water leaving clean tissue, whereas in a contusion, extravasated clotted blood adheres stubbornly.
steps.say: To distinguish a bruise from lividity, make a cut: in lividity, blood washes away easily with water; in a bruise, clotted blood sticks to tissues.

left.title: Postmortem lividity
points: Occurs exclusively in dependent uncompressed parts
Blood is strictly intravascular within intact capillaries
Incision reveals blood that washes away with water
Epidermis intact; no swelling or abrasion

right.title: Antemortem contusion (Bruise)
points: Can occur anywhere on the body where trauma struck
Blood is extravasated into subcutaneous tissues
Incision reveals clotted blood that cannot be washed
Associated with swelling, tissue damage, or abrasion

steps.title: Biochemical mechanism of rigor mortis
steps.tx: Following a variable period of primary muscular flaccidity, **rigor mortis biochemical stiffening** develops across all voluntary and involuntary muscles. Muscular relaxation requires adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to detach myosin cross-bridges from actin filaments. Following death, cellular ATP synthesis ceases. When cellular ATP concentrations plummet below eighty-five percent of normal, actin and myosin bind irreversibly into a rigid actomyosin complex.
steps.say: Rigor mortis occurs because dying muscles run out of ATP energy, causing actin and myosin to lock irreversibly into a stiff muscle gel.

nodes.label: Loss of aerobic respiration halts ATP regeneration
Cellular ATP drops below 85% critical threshold
Myosin heads lock irreversibly onto actin filaments
Formation of rigid actomyosin gel produces skeletal stiffening

steps.title: The Nysten rule and anatomical progression
steps.tx: Rigor mortis involves involuntary muscles first (the myocardium becomes rigid within one hour), before spreading across voluntary skeletal muscles according to the **Nysten rule progression order**. Rigor manifests craniocaudally: appearing in the eyelids, lower jaw, and face, descending into the neck, thorax, upper limbs, abdomen, lower limbs, and concluding in the toes. When resolving, rigor disappears in the identical craniocaudal order.
steps.say: Under Nysten's rule, rigor mortis spreads downward from the face, jaw, and neck to the chest, arms, abdomen, legs, and toes, disappearing in the same order.

nodes.label: Involuntary heart muscle and pupillary sphincters (1 hour)
Eyelids, lower jaw, facial expression muscles, and neck (1 to 3 hours)
Chest, shoulders, arms, forearms, and hands (4 to 8 hours)
Abdomen, pelvis, thighs, legs, and toes (8 to 12 hours)

steps.title: Timeline of rigor mortis in the Indian climate
steps.tx: In tropical climates, examiners apply the **rule of twelves Indian rigor timeline** to estimate postmortem intervals. In northern and central India, rigor mortis requires approximately twelve hours to develop fully across the entire body, persists fully established for twelve hours, and takes twelve hours to disappear as autolysis breaks down actomyosin bonds, yielding a thirty-six-hour total cycle in winter.
steps.say: In India, rigor mortis follows the rule of twelve: twelve hours to develop, twelve hours to persist, and twelve hours to disappear as decomposition begins.

rows: Spreading stiffness descending from jaw to feet
All joints locked rigid; body can be lifted like a board
Softening commences in face and descends toward toes
High heat accelerates onset and rapid decomposition

steps.title: Cadaveric spasm: Instantaneous postmortem rigidity
steps.tx: In dramatic circumstances, **cadaveric spasm instantaneous rigidity** locks a group of voluntary muscles into contraction at the precise instant of death, completely bypassing the initial phase of primary flaccidity. Occurring under intense emotional excitement, physical struggle, or extreme exhaustion immediately prior to death, cadaveric spasm preserves the final antemortem act: grasping grass or weeds in drowning, or clutching a firearm in suicide.
steps.say: Cadaveric spasm is instant stiffening at the moment of death during violent struggle or drowning, freezing a weapon or weeds tightly in the hand.

left.title: Rigor mortis
points: Preceded by primary muscular flaccidity
Involves every voluntary and involuntary muscle
Driven by generalized postmortem ATP depletion
Can be broken mechanically and will not return

right.title: Cadaveric spasm
points: Immediate onset at the instant of death
Confined to specific voluntary muscle groups (hands)
Driven by severe emotional tension and exhaustion
Incontrovertible proof of an antemortem act

steps.title: Heat stiffening and cold stiffening
steps.tx: Examiners must distinguish true rigor from physical mimics, notably **heat stiffening and cold stiffening**. Heat stiffening occurs when a body is exposed to intense fire or scalding fluids exceeding sixty-five degrees Celsius, causing thermal denaturation and coagulation of muscle proteins that locks the body into a pugilistic boxer's attitude. Cold stiffening occurs when ambient temperatures drop below freezing, turning synovial fluids and subcutaneous fat solid.
steps.say: Heat stiffening cooks muscle proteins in fire, creating a boxer stance. Cold stiffening freezes body fluids; both must be distinguished from rigor mortis.

rows: Develops gradually; preceded by flaccid phase
Extreme emotional excitement / struggle at death
Locks hand tightly onto weapon or drowning weeds
Thermal protein coagulation at > 65 deg C
Produces pugilistic boxing stance with charred skin
Freezing of body water, fat, and synovial fluid
Joints crackle when flexed; thaws in warm mortuary
